title: NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 Achieves up to 2x Blackwell Ultra Performance in MLPerf Training v6.1 | NVIDIA Technical Blog
gist: In its MLPerf Training v6.1 debut, NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 posted the fastest time to train on six of seven benchmarks with 1.4x-2x per-GPU gains over an optimized GB300 NVL72, the largest (2x) on the communication-heavy DeepSeek-V3 671B MoE model, while a 10,240-GPU GB300 cluster took the absolute fastest DeepSeek-V3 time. NVIDIA frames the result as proof of day-one CUDA software maturity, highlights the new Qwen 3.5 397B GRPO RL post-training benchmark, and stresses post-ship software gains (unverified reruns up to 2.4x vs GB300's v6.1 submission) and an 80% share of closed-division submissions.

insights.claim: In MLPerf Training v6.1, NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 delivered the fastest time to train on six of seven benchmarks and up to 2x per-GPU performance versus an optimized GB300 NVL72 baseline, with 1.4x-1.6x gains on the remaining workloads.
insights.speaker: Farshad Ghodsian
insights.so_what: Sets the Rubin-over-Blackwell Ultra training uplift at roughly 1.4x-2x per GPU — a benchmark for pricing Rubin ASP premiums and Blackwell residual value.
insights.quote: While the platform is consistently 1.4x to 1.6x faster across the rest of the suite, the generational advantage widens even further for the massive DeepSeek-V3 benchmark.

insights.claim: Vera Rubin NVL72 trained DeepSeek-V3 671B MoE in 4.14 minutes on 1,024 GPUs across 16 racks versus 8.03 minutes for GB300 NVL72 at the identical scale — roughly 2x per GPU, the largest generational gain of the round.
insights.speaker: Farshad Ghodsian
insights.so_what: The biggest Rubin gains land on frontier-scale MoE training, the workload hyperscalers and labs spend most on.
insights.locator: DeepSeek-V3 671B: 2x per GPU on the hardest workload

insights.claim: NVIDIA argues the generational advantage of Vera Rubin over GB300 grows with model size and communication intensity, because expert parallelism in MoE models turns every iteration into all-to-all communication where fabric efficiency directly sets time to train.
insights.speaker: Farshad Ghodsian
insights.so_what: As frontier models shift further to large MoE, interconnect (NVLink, scale-out networking) becomes a larger share of the value — supportive of NVIDIA's networking attach.
insights.quote: The largest gain lands on the largest, most communication-heavy model.

insights.claim: NVIDIA frames halving time to train as roughly doubling the number of experiments an AI team can run per quarter, positioning experiment throughput as the driver of model quality and the economic case for upgrading GPUs.
insights.speaker: Farshad Ghodsian
insights.so_what: This is the upgrade-cycle sales argument: watch whether labs actually replace Blackwell quickly on iteration-speed grounds.
insights.quote: Halving time to train roughly doubles how many experiments a team can run in a quarter, and experiment throughput is what moves model quality.
insights.locator: Vera Rubin NVL72 trained the benchmark in 4.14 minutes

insights.claim: A 10,240-GPU GB300 NVL72 cluster (160 racks, one training job) posted the absolute fastest DeepSeek-V3 671B time of MLPerf Training v6.1 at 1.38 minutes, so NVIDIA platforms hold the fastest time to train on every v6.1 benchmark.
insights.speaker: Farshad Ghodsian
insights.so_what: Blackwell Ultra remains the scale workhorse even as Rubin ramps — supports continued Blackwell demand alongside Rubin.
insights.locator: At a larger scale, GB300 NVL72 produced the fastest absolute result

insights.claim: Vera Rubin NVL72 maintained above 97% scaling efficiency on DeepSeek-V3 when scaling from 256 to 1,024 GPUs (4 to 16 racks).
insights.speaker: Farshad Ghodsian
insights.so_what: Near-linear multi-rack scaling reduces the penalty of building larger clusters, supporting bigger Rubin deployments per customer.
insights.locator: This cohesive design translates directly to efficiency.

insights.claim: Vera Rubin NVL72 connects 72 GPUs and 36 CPUs over a copper NVLink 6 spine delivering 3.6 TB/s per GPU and 260 TB/s per rack, and scales out via ConnectX-9 SuperNICs over Quantum-X800 InfiniBand or Spectrum-X Ethernet with adaptive routing and congestion control to hide bursty MoE all-to-all traffic.
insights.speaker: Farshad Ghodsian
insights.so_what: Copper in-rack plus NVIDIA's own NICs and switches means networking content per rack stays NVIDIA-captured; relevant for copper cable/connector suppliers and rival networking vendors.
insights.quote: Every result above is also a networking result.
insights.locator: NVLink, Quantum-X and Spectrum-X: Co-designed networking

insights.claim: NVIDIA keeps a consistent 72-GPU NVL72 domain across generations so customers get predictable performance jumps each cycle without changing their operating model, which lowers switching friction for upgrading within the NVIDIA ecosystem.
insights.speaker: Farshad Ghodsian
insights.so_what: A stable rack form factor across Blackwell to Rubin is a lock-in mechanism that eases annual-cadence upgrades.
insights.quote: Each cycle simply delivers more compute and bandwidth across the same consistent fabric.
insights.locator: Because the NVL72 architecture provides a consistent 72-GPU domain

themes.theme: RL post-training benchmark and Vera CPU

insights.claim: MLPerf Training v6.1 added its first agentic LLM reinforcement learning post-training benchmark (Qwen 3.5 397B GRPO), where Vera Rubin NVL72 led at 10.44 minutes on 1,024 GPUs versus 13.78 minutes for GB300 NVL72, and also submitted with vLLM (10.94 minutes) alongside NeMo RL with TensorRT-LLM.
insights.speaker: Farshad Ghodsian
insights.so_what: RL post-training is now a standardized benchmark category — compute demand is shifting toward post-training, not just pretraining.
insights.locator: Post-training arrives, and Vera Rubin leads it

insights.claim: NVIDIA states that post-training has become the critical differentiator for agentic accuracy, and that GRPO-style RL stresses systems by forcing constant, massive weight migrations between inference and training engines.
insights.speaker: Farshad Ghodsian
insights.so_what: If post-training is the differentiator, compute spend keeps growing even if pretraining scaling plateaus.
insights.quote: Post-training has emerged as the critical differentiator for agentic accuracy, making the GRPO workload uniquely demanding.
insights.locator: MLPerf Training v6.1 adds its first agentic LLM reinforcement learning

insights.claim: Because simulating agentic RL environments (tool calls, code, API validations) is CPU-bound, NVIDIA positions the Vera CPU as integral to RL training, with a single Vera CPU rack of 256 CPUs sustaining more than 22,500 concurrent RL environments.
insights.speaker: Farshad Ghodsian
insights.so_what: Agentic RL creates a new CPU demand vector that NVIDIA aims to capture with its own Arm CPU — a potential headwind for x86 server CPU share in AI clusters.
insights.locator: Teaching these models to observe, reason, and act

insights.claim: Unverified NVIDIA reruns with a newer software stack on the same hardware cut Vera Rubin NVL72 time to train to 6.140 min on Llama 3.1 8B (from 7.162), 8.080 min on gpt-oss 20B (from 11.213) and 1.628 min on DLRMv4 (from 2.829) — up to 2.4x faster than GB300's MLPerf v6.1 submission; GB300 itself also improved (e.g. DLRMv4 3.871 to 2.940 min).
insights.speaker: Farshad Ghodsian
insights.so_what: Software keeps lifting installed-base performance, an argument for longer useful lives of GPU fleets (relevant to depreciation debates); note results are unverified by MLCommons.
insights.locator: Continuous software optimization: Unlocking faster pretraining

insights.claim: NVIDIA argues continuous CUDA software optimization makes its infrastructure faster after it ships, extending platform productive lifetime and revenue-generating potential.
insights.speaker: Farshad Ghodsian
insights.so_what: Directly counters the bear case that rapid GPU cadence makes prior generations obsolete quickly — key to neocloud/hyperscaler depreciation assumptions.
insights.quote: The infrastructure gets faster after it ships, and the improvements continue to arrive, extending the platform’s productive lifetime and revenue generating potential.
insights.locator: That is what a mature software stack means for customers.

insights.claim: Thinking Machines Lab built an NVFP4 training recipe with custom kernels for its Inkling 2 Small model on GB300 NVL72 (NVFP4 for forward-pass MoE GEMMs, MXFP8 for gradients), speeding pretraining and fine-tuning by 8% and reinforcement learning by 20% versus full MXFP8 with minimal accuracy impact.
insights.speaker: Farshad Ghodsian
insights.so_what: Low-precision (FP4) training is moving into production at frontier labs, raising effective compute per GPU on existing hardware.
insights.locator: Because the CUDA platform is highly programmable

insights.claim: 80% of all MLPerf Training v6.1 closed-division submissions ran on NVIDIA platforms across 20 partner organizations, and NVIDIA was the only vendor to submit on all seven benchmarks.
insights.speaker: Farshad Ghodsian
insights.so_what: Competitors (AMD, custom ASICs) still largely absent from full-suite training benchmarks — evidence of NVIDIA's continued training moat.
insights.locator: An ecosystem that shipped on day one

insights.claim: Azure's 2,560-node, 10,240-GPU GB200 NVL72 submission tied NVIDIA's 10,240-GPU GB300 NVL72 run as the largest clusters of MLPerf Training v6.1, and Vera Rubin NVL72 systems are already generally available through cloud infrastructure partners.
insights.speaker: Farshad Ghodsian
insights.so_what: Rubin being generally available in cloud by Nov 2026 signals the ramp is on schedule; Microsoft is operating 10k-GPU-scale Blackwell clusters.

insights.claim: Firmus used AI-driven kernel generation with automated performance testing and mathematical validation to post the fastest GB300 8-GPU result of MLPerf Training v6.1, training GPT-OSS 20B in 52.90 minutes and Llama 3.1 8B in 52.40 minutes.
insights.speaker: Farshad Ghodsian
insights.so_what: AI-generated kernels are beginning to deliver benchmark-leading results, a trend that could compress the CUDA-expertise moat over time.
insights.locator: Partners are also pushing the limits of the architecture
